activity.title: This is not a generic startup school post.. Here were my favorite parts: First - We snuck into the Stripe after party (after registration had closed) by using using one guy’s ticket. (The point here is if you want something you can always find a way to get it) I think the most valuable thing I got was when I was invited to an exclusive invite only event with only 10 people with the founder of Alex.com (Aaron) and YC partner Nicolas Dessaigne. This was especially interesting because I asked them two specific questions that I think are key to any successful company. “How do you hire people smarter than you?” “How do you get your first customer?” Aaron didn’t actually answer the first question, it was rather vague but Nicholas shared some perspective which lit a spark on me . It comes down to two things “conviction of the founder.” “And accepting that people are smarter than you” - imagine that in a French accent. The second question was something I had asked all the founders at YC startup school. One interesting one was “I flew to Louisiana in person for my first demo” - Bild AI Aaron’s was similar his Ai was broken so he hand transcribe what the Ai was supposed to do after it broke on his first demo. It’s not standard to anyone, the only rule is ship and talk about it loudly to anyone who will Listen . The whole point of this is to open source as much closed knowledge as possible, since unfortunately not everyone has access to these people. I’m curious what your answers are to those two questions. Also shout to Enes Yilmaz and Ali Tariq for being born. this is us at the aforementioned Stripe party. ...more

UPDATE: The fundraising goal has been reached, and the fundraiser is now closed. Thank you to everyone who made this possible. Hello everyone! My name is Yerulan, and I'm from Kazakhstan. I recently graduated from Nazarbayev University, and I'm excited to share that I've been admitted to the MSc in Computer Science program at ETH Zurich. I come from a low-income family in Kazakhstan, and most of my education so far has been possible because of programs that reduced the role of finances, from Nazarbayev Intellectual Schools and support at Nazarbayev University as a student in a socially vulnerable category to a fully funded research internship at MBZUAI. These opportunities made it possible for me to focus on learning. With this support, I was able to graduate from Nazarbayev University ranked 1st in my Computer Science cohort. I now have the opportunity to continue my studies at ETH Zurich, but the financial barrier to taking this next step is much higher. The main challenge is covering the initial period. As a non-EU/EFTA student, I cannot work outside ETH during my first six months in Switzerland. In the meantime, I'm actively looking for Teaching Assistant positions within my department, but I still need support to make the beginning of my studies possible before I can become more financially self-sustaining. I am raising CHF 10,000 (approximately USD 12.4k or KZT 5.8M) to help cover: - six months of minimum living expenses in Zurich: CHF 1,750 × 6 = CHF 10,500 - one semester of tuition: CHF 2,190 - airfare / initial travel costs: approximately CHF 300 Total: approximately CHF 13,000. In the long term, I want to use what I learn in Computer Science and ML for problems relevant to Kazakhstan and Central Asia. My previous research focused on rainfall-runoff modeling and flood prediction for Kazakhstani river basins, and I want to keep building skills that can be useful for climate and NLP challenges back home. Thank you! ...more ...more

AI playing Minecraft is cool, but we wanted to build something that has never been done. Claude Code in Minecraft That Can Generate Any Mob you can think of with custom -skills, texture and abilities. One Step Closer to AGI For the Y Combinator x Browser Use Agent Hackathon, we turned Claude into a live, malicious game engine. Meet BrowseCraft. It is an AI agent that intercepts raw game data, hallucinates entirely new enemies, codes their custom abilities on the fly, and injects them into the server live while you play. The best part? It has zero hardcoded vanilla bias. Because BrowseCraft reads raw entity registries, it is completely data-agnostic. That means you can drop it into literally ANY custom Minecraft modpack. It instantly parses the new mechanics, cross-breeds assets, and invents custom nightmares using that specific mod's ecosystem. The video below shows it mutating vanilla Minecraft, but the architecture is built to infect anything. This is where I need your help: Drop your most chaotic, complex Minecraft modpacks in the comments. I am going to let the agent loose on the top suggestions tonight and post the results. What should we infect next? 👇 #YCHackathon #BrowserUseHackathon #AIAgents #Claude #GameDev #Engineering ...more

I did Y Combinator with founders of Legora , Reducto , and Greptile . Today, W24 has raised close to $2 billion. Two years ago, none of us had it figured out. Nobody in that room could tell you who was going to make it. Not the partners, not the investors circling demo day, definitely not us. But I spent that batch watching the other teams, and it taught me more than most of the advice ever did. 1. The idea you apply with is rarely the one that wins. Some companies are stuck in pivot hell, trying to figure out what to build. Half the batch looked completely different by just demo day. 2. You also can't pick the winner from a demo. I was in a group with Reducto and Raindrop . Incredible founders, but on paper, none of us looked obviously destined for anything. The teams who took off just learned faster, and the market they picked mattered less. 3. The people matter more than the company. The startup you meet in the batch might not exist in a year, but the person will. It’s why the batch still pays off two years later. - Some of the founders I met in W24 are Momentic customers now. - Some have grown into people who shape what we build next. - Some are just the people I text when a six-figure deal falls apart and I need someone who actually gets it. So if you're in the batch right now: you have no idea which of you will become the next billion-dollar company. Neither did we. But be generous with the teams around you, and stay in touch long after demo day. In a couple years, any one of them could be your best customer, your closest advisor, or the only person who understands exactly what you're going through. I’m grateful I got to learn from that batch, and that two years later I still get to call some of them my closest friends.

I recently found an old article about me from when I was still a student at Berkeley, and at the time, I wrote this: “I was always entrepreneurial, but I just didn’t realize it until I reached college.” That still feels pretty accurate. I didn’t arrive at Berkeley with a five-year plan to start companies or become a venture capitalist. I just knew I liked building things, chasing ideas that seemed interesting, helping talented people achieve their potential, and bringing people together. Then, during my first semester, I entered a Berkeley entrepreneurship competition (judged by successful entrepreneurs) with an edtech idea called LectConnect and won an award. It was one of the first times I saw entrepreneurship as something I could actually do. From there, I started spending more time trying to find other student founders. There were no clubs for startups, so I decided to build the community I wished had existed when I first arrived. Reading that article again made me think about how many students are probably in the same position today. They may already have all the instincts of a founder - curiosity, ambition, a tendency to question how things work, an urge to build something better - without having a name for any of it yet. Sometimes all it takes is the right event, class, club, competition, co-founder, or community to make that possibility visible. That’s one of the things I love most about Berkeley. There are thousands of students on campus right now who haven’t figured out what they’re capable of yet. It feels great to “go for it.” Here’s me on the New Year Stock Exchange as a student in ~2011 presenting one of the top 50 startups globally at the Kairos Summit. If you’re at Berkeley and starting to build something, especially once the idea starts becoming real, reach out. You don’t need to have everything figured out. You don’t need the perfect pitch deck or a company that already looks “venture-backable.” The House Fund exists to support Berkeley founders early, and we’re always happy to be a resource - whether that means feedback, an introduction, advice, or eventually a check.

Two weeks into my internship at Getz Pharma, working in Marketing and Sales at the new Astola head office, and the halfway point feels like a good moment to share what I have learned so far. Most of my time has gone to Sem-P, our semaglutide, working alongside the team behind it. What has struck me most is how much clinical depth underpins commercial decisions. Coming from a biology degree meant I could follow the science from day one, and that has proved far more valuable than I anticipated. I have also been given real room to contribute. My marketing ideas were taken seriously and discussed properly, which speaks to how the team operates. Everyone in the room is invited to have a view, and that is not something I took for granted as an intern. That openness carries into how the work gets done. Marketing presents the coming months to sales managers, sales respond with what they are seeing in the field, and the plans that emerge are stronger for it. Cross functional collaboration reads very differently on paper than it looks in practice. The scope widens from here. This week I am learning business strategy and its frameworks, and later in the internship I move into production and quality control, which should give me a full view from how these medicines are made through to how they reach patients. Three weeks to go, and plenty still to learn. Grateful to Getz Pharma for the opportunity!!
